questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
When choosing a destination, I knew I wanted something within Europe (partly due to the Erasmus agreement among other things), however, I also wanted to experience a different culture from what I was used to in Copenhagen. I feel, I found this in Milan. The city is super nice and have so many things to offer, and the location invites for travels in the nearby regions. The culture is quite different from the Danish, which I find super interesting and there were plenty of things to learn about this new environment. 

Further, I of course also valued the academic level of the university, where I could find English subjects that interested me. Thought the semester, I was quite satisfied with the classes I attended, and it was a great bonus for me that I found courses which could substitute mandatory courses at Copenhagen University.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: When all this is said, I do not think that the destination is the most important aspect of an exchange. As long as you arrive with an open mind and you are excited for the challenge to come, the destination will be secondary. I absolutely loved my exchange semester, but this was mainly due to all the people I met and the experiences we had together.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: In Milan, or Italy in general, they are much more chilled and relaxed than we tend to be here in Denmark, and therefore, the information came quite late. However, I was staying at a student residency where I was able to check in the day I arrived, which made the arrival super easy. Regarding university, courses and so on, the relevant information came a week or two before classes started.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: At the student residency, I was meet by the receptionist. Although his English proficiency was limited, there was no problem getting my key and finding my room. Here I soon meet Italian and other international students, who could help if there was some kind of problem of difficulty. At the university, people were also kind to help getting around and understanding the new educational system.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There was not a lot of orientation upon arrival, but I got all the necessary information, and enough for me to begin the semester. It is a process of learning by doing and not to be embarrassed to ask the questions that might arise.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: For me, it was super easy. I received an email from the university asking whether I was interested in student housing, which I accepted. After a few weeks, I received another email with a link to a website where I could choose my preferred residency. I would definitely recommend living in a student residency, both because it was super cheap and because it was very social and many of my close friends were other students I met there.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The residency where I lived was located a bit outside the city centre, which at times was a little annoying. However, it was not more than 20 minutes by bike or bus to the university faculty and 30 minutes to the city centre.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: One downside to the residency was the single large common kitchen. Each student brought all their cooking supplies (pots, pans and so on) down to the kitchen, and the kitchen could get super crowded at night. However, we quickly learned to cook at "Danish hours" around 19 and then the kitchen would be close to empty. A good thing about the one large common kitchen, was that we often cooked together and had large common dinners which was very cozy.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The registration for the courses was just a few weeks before the semester started. It was very easy to register, and also to get the courses moved around at a later point if necessary.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Once you are accepted at the university, you get a login to a personalised student website where much of the information can be found. On the front page there was a link to the course registration. Once you register here, you will be admitted to the course and you do not have to wait for an approval mail. Then you can download an app, where you find the timetable and any news if, for example, the lecture is cancelled or moved to another room.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There is an Erasmus coordination (Massimo) who helps the international students with anything university/course related. It was super easy to just send him an email if there was a question, but it was also possible to set a meeting with him, if something more in depth was needed. I took a course at a different faculty, which I at first did not have access to, but in that situation, I got all the help I needed.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: One of the courses I had gotten pre-approved, ended up not being registered as a course that semester. However, I had gotten a few additional courses pre-approved in advance in case anything like this would happen, and could therefore just choose one of the other courses. Thus, I ended up with the classes I wanted, three of which I have been able to get approved as mandatory courses at Copenhagen University.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It was very easy to register for courses, so I do not think this should be a big concern for future students. Many of my friends also decided to swap from one course to another later in the semester without a problem. As mentioned, they are much more chilled and relaxed concerning these formalities in Italy than what we are used to in Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, I was quite satisfied. Of course some courses were more interesting than others, but that is to be expected. The only thing which could be a bit challenging at times, was the structure of an academic year. At the faculty of economics and social sciences, they use trimesters rather than semesters, meaning I had to take 30 ECTS points in a shorter amount of time (one is supposed to pass 20 ECTS point each trimester). It was not a major problem, but keeping up with five different classes could be a challenge at times.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: In general, the courses were easier than what I have been used to in Copenhagen. I was challenged in especially one class, but the rest did not require as much work and effort as I expected even if it was masters courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: For each of my five courses, we had two lectures a week for two hours (in total, four hours per course). We did not have any tutorial classes, but in some lectures there was time dedicated to solving problems and so on. For the most parts there were not any “take home assignments”, however, in one of the courses, there was a mandatory group presentation as part of the final grade. In some classes, we could also take a mid-term exam, which would make the final exam easier.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Game Theory - 6 ECTS (substituting microeconomics III)
Business History - 6 ECTS (substituting economic history)
Time Series Analysis - 6 ECTS (substituting econometrics II)
Ethics Economics - 6 ECTS (elective)
Sustainable Development in Global Trade (WTO) Law - 6 ECTS (an elective law course)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would definitely recommend taking the three courses I got approved as mandatory courses in Copenhagen. Time Series Analysis was a bit challenging, but in the end I think it has been worth it. I found Game Theory very interesting, and the professor teaching was very motivating, dedicated and good at her job.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: When I first arrived at the student residency, I spend a bit of money on different kitchen supplies. I was not expecting this, however, considering the monthly rent, I do not think I am entitled to complain.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Going out for dinner was cheaper than I expected, but this also meant that I went to cafes and restaurants quite often.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were different local sports clubs and such, but it could be a little complicated at times. However, the Erasmus exchange group ESN was arranging many different events and sports teams which you could sign up for.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The ESN group arranged everything from city tours and sport nights to pub crawling and nights out at different clubs. Further, they also planned trips to different cities and places around Italy. 

I went to these kinds of events in the beginning, however, after some time and after developing a group of friends, we attended the events less and less. But it was nice and reassuring to know that there is always some kind of social event or gathering.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I did not attend many planned activities in larger groups throughout the semester. However, I really enjoyed playing paddle tennis with my friends from time to time. It was super easy and convenient to rent the courts in the morning, on days classes started at 12 or later.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Milan is very well connected to the rest of Italy both by train and bus routes (which you can find at very low prices). I would definitely recommend taking advantage of this on the weekends either just as a day trip or to stay a night. Some of my favourite places to visit was Bologna, Turin, Lake Como, Portofino and Lugano in Switzerland. 

The weekends I spend in Milan, I really liked going to different antique/vintage markets around the city and just explore different areas (Navigli, Porta Venezia, Brera, China town).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Of course it will take more than half a year to really adopt to a new culture, and for me there was definitely also a language barrier. However, I did not find it difficult to live with the culture and I have a much better understanding of the culture and way of life. I feel that I quickly got used to and adjusted to the way locals interact with each other and the daily lifestyle.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: My greatest tip for socialising with local students is to live at a student residency or an other type of shared housing. Here you see people everyday and it is super easy to start a conversation in the kitchen or common areas.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I did not find the cultural differences to be all that challenging, but if I have to mention one it would be with the lack of organisation and structure. At times, this could be a bit frustrating but I quickly got used to it, and sometimes even saw it as an advantage.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I absolutely love the Italian cuisine, and this alone has been a great appreciation of mine. All though I at times found the lack of organisation and structure challenging, I have really come to enjoy a more relaxed mindset without too many worries.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) do not stress too much about choosing the right courses and such, you will receive the needed information and there is always the possibility of making alternations later on 2) be open to meet new people anywhere and anytime 3) just go on trips, attend events and enjoy it as long as it lasts

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think I have already mentioned the most important, but get the subscription to public transportation in the beginning, and do not worry about getting an official fiscal code, the one you can get online is enough.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: As cliche as it sounds, the most rewarding part of my exchange was all the amazing people I met and close friendships I developed. It was quite special living abroad for such a relatively short amount of time, and I feel I have developed so many close relationships in a very short amount of time.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To me, the greatest challenge was to make time for everything I wanted to experience while living there, and balancing studies and social life.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Enjoy :))

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
